questions.q: In leader-follower replication, why do writes go only to the leader?
options: A single write point gives one authoritative ordering of changes
Followers lack the storage engine needed to persist writes
Network routes to follower nodes are read-optimized and silently drop writes
The leader holds the only copy of the table schema
questions.explanation: Funnelling writes through one node yields a single serialized change log that every follower can replay identically, avoiding conflicts. Followers are fully capable engines; they are simply kept read-only by design.

questions.q: What does synchronous replication guarantee that asynchronous does not?
options: The leader can serve reads without touching its local disk at all
Followers apply writes in a different order for load balancing
An acknowledged write already exists on a follower, surviving leader loss
Replication traffic is encrypted between the leader and followers
questions.explanation: The leader waits for follower confirmation before acknowledging, so any committed write is durable on at least two nodes. That is what makes zero data loss on failover possible.

questions.q: What is replication lag?
options: The measured round-trip network latency between any two replicas in the cluster
The delay between a write on the leader and its visibility on a follower
The time a follower needs to complete its initial full data copy
The pause writes experience while a new follower is added
questions.explanation: Lag measures how far behind a follower's applied state is from the leader's, combining shipping and apply time. It is why replica reads can return stale data.

questions.q: Why add read replicas to a database?
options: They accept writes in parallel, multiplying write throughput
They validate each transaction a second time, catching corruption
They shrink the dataset by storing only frequently read rows
They spread read traffic across copies, offloading the primary
questions.explanation: Replicas hold full copies, so read queries can fan out across them while the leader concentrates on writes. They add no write capacity, since all writes still funnel through the leader.

questions.q: A follower crashes and restarts. How does it typically catch up?
options: It performs a full copy of the leader's data from scratch every time
It promotes itself to leader until it has verified its local data
It requests changes after the last log position it had applied
It serves stale reads permanently until an operator reseeds it
questions.explanation: The follower records its last applied log offset on disk and asks the leader to resume streaming from there, so only the missed changes travel. A full resync is needed only if that log has been discarded.

questions.q: What is failover in a replicated database?
options: Promoting a follower to leader after the current leader becomes unavailable
Redirecting reads to the leader when followers are overloaded
Archiving the write-ahead log into cold object storage for later disaster recovery
Splitting the leader into two nodes to double write capacity
questions.explanation: Failover restores write availability by electing a replica as the new leader and repointing clients to it. The old leader must be fenced off so it cannot keep accepting writes.

questions.q: Why is asynchronous replication the common default despite its risks?
options: It guarantees zero data loss without any latency penalty on commits
Asynchronous followers can also accept writes, adding cluster capacity
It compresses the replication stream better than synchronous modes do
Writes commit without waiting on followers, keeping latency low and tolerating slow replicas
questions.explanation: Commit latency stays independent of replica health and network distance, so one lagging follower cannot stall the leader. The trade is a window of unreplicated writes that failover can lose.

questions.q: In multi-leader replication, when do write conflicts arise?
options: Whenever any two writes occur anywhere in the cluster at the same second
When the same record is modified concurrently on different leaders
Only when a follower applies replicated changes out of order
When a leader's clock drifts more than the replication interval
questions.explanation: Each leader accepts its write locally, so two updates to the same item made before replication reaches the other node collide and must be reconciled. Writes to different records never conflict.

questions.q: A user posts a comment, refreshes, and the comment is gone, then reappears. Likely cause?
options: The comment table's index was rebuilt between the two page loads
An anti-spam filter quarantined the comment until moderation finished
The browser cached the pre-comment page and replayed it on refresh
Successive reads hit different replicas, some behind the leader
questions.explanation: With asynchronous replicas, one request can land on a caught-up node and the next on a lagging one, so data appears to move backwards. Read-your-writes routing or monotonic-read stickiness fixes it.

questions.q: How does a 'read-your-writes' guarantee typically get implemented?
options: All reads go to the leader for every user at all times
Route the writer's subsequent reads to the leader or a caught-up replica
Followers block all reads until every pending write is applied
Every write is duplicated into a per-user client cache that overrides later reads
questions.explanation: Only the user who just wrote needs the fresh copy, so the system pins their reads to the leader briefly, or picks a replica whose applied position covers their write token. Everyone else keeps using replicas.

questions.q: Why can promoting an asynchronous follower during failover lose data?
options: Writes the old leader acknowledged may not have reached the promoted follower
Followers store their data in a lossy columnar format until promotion
Promotion wipes the follower's replication log to guarantee a clean start
All clients must reconnect during promotion, and their in-flight reads get counted as lost writes
questions.explanation: Asynchronous commits are acknowledged before shipping, so anything still in flight when the leader dies is simply absent from the new leader. That unreplicated window is the effective RPO.

questions.q: Two leaders concurrently update the same profile field. 'Last write wins' resolves it. What is the hidden cost?
options: Both writes are kept forever, doubling storage for that record
Conflict resolution acquires a global lock, briefly pausing writes across the whole cluster
One acknowledged write is silently discarded based on unreliable timestamps
Clocks must be perfectly synchronized or the cluster halts
questions.explanation: LWW always converges, but it converges by throwing away a write the client was told succeeded, and clock skew can make the older update win. Nothing halts, the loss is just invisible.

questions.q: What problem does a replication quorum (W + R > N) solve?
options: It compresses replication traffic exchanged between the write and read node sets
Read and write sets overlap, so a read sees at least one latest copy
It elects a permanent leader without any coordination service
It caps replica count so lag can never exceed one write
questions.explanation: If writes touch W nodes and reads touch R nodes out of N, requiring W + R > N forces at least one node in common, so the reader can observe the newest version rather than only stale ones.

questions.q: During a network blip, two nodes both believe they are leader ('split brain'). Chief danger?
options: Reads slow down noticeably because clients must query both leaders on every request
The cluster permanently loses the ability to elect any leader
Followers refuse to replicate from either node, freezing all traffic
Both accept conflicting writes, diverging the dataset irrecoverably
questions.explanation: Two authoritative write paths produce two histories that cannot be automatically merged once the partition heals. Quorum-based election and fencing tokens exist to prevent this.

questions.q: Why do many systems use semi-synchronous replication (one sync follower, rest async)?
options: It bounds data loss without paying full synchronous latency on every follower
It doubles the effective read throughput served by the single synchronous follower
It lets the asynchronous followers skip conflict detection entirely
It removes the need for failover automation and monitoring
questions.explanation: Waiting on exactly one replica guarantees each commit exists on two nodes while the commit path only ever waits on the fastest peer, not on every distant or slow follower.

questions.q: A monitoring dashboard shows follower lag climbing steadily under normal traffic. Most likely cause?
options: The leader batches its log shipping into hourly windows under the default configuration
TLS handshakes are being repeated for every replicated row
The follower applies the single-threaded log slower than the leader generates it
Lag metrics are cumulative and always climb until a restart
questions.explanation: The leader commits with many parallel connections while replay is often serial, so once apply throughput falls below write throughput the backlog grows without bound. Parallel apply or lighter writes are the fix.

questions.q: An RPO of zero (no lost writes) is mandated across two regions 80 ms apart. What is the unavoidable consequence?
options: Reads served from the remote region become inconsistent and must therefore be disabled
Zero RPO across separated regions is impossible under any replication scheme
Every commit pays cross-region latency, since writes must be durable in both
The follower region can never be promoted without operator sign-off
questions.explanation: Losing nothing when a region dies means the other region must already hold the write, so each commit includes at least one cross-region round trip. Zero RPO buys durability with latency.

questions.q: Why is automatic failover dangerous with aggressive (short) failure-detection timeouts?
options: A slow but healthy leader may be demoted, and repeated flapping can lose or fork writes
Short timeouts overload DNS, since each liveness check requires a fresh lookup
Followers cannot be promoted more than once per hour safely
The write-ahead log truncates whenever detection fires, corrupting replicas
questions.explanation: A GC pause or traffic spike is indistinguishable from death over a short timeout, so the system promotes needlessly. Each unnecessary promotion drops in-flight writes and risks two live leaders.

questions.q: Compared with last-write-wins, what do version vectors add to multi-leader conflict handling?
options: They synchronize physical clocks so timestamps become trustworthy
They serialize all writes through a single elected arbiter node
They shrink conflict metadata down to a single integer per record
They detect concurrent updates so conflicts surface instead of being silently dropped
questions.explanation: Per-replica counters establish causality, distinguishing a genuine overwrite from two concurrent edits. Concurrent versions are kept as siblings for the application or a CRDT to merge, at the cost of extra metadata.

questions.q: You must scale writes for a workload with heavy per-record contention across regions. Why does multi-leader replication help less than hoped?
options: Multi-leader clusters cap out at exactly two regions in practice
Contended records conflict constantly, and resolution costs erase the write gains
Each leader must hold the full dataset in memory to accept writes
Cross-region links cannot carry replication and client traffic together
questions.explanation: Extra leaders only add throughput when writes touch disjoint records. With hot contended keys, every region's write collides, and merge logic plus lost updates cost more than the parallelism gains. Partitioning by key locality is the better fix.
